Title: AKU research among top 2018 emergency medicine studies
NewsSummary: The University's research was recognised in an annual review of research in the field.
NewsContent:
The University's research on respiratory distress in children has been recognised as one of the top global emergency medicine (EM) articles of 2018 by the Global Emergency Medicine Literature Review (GEMLR). 

GEMLR is a US-based group of EM researchers who identify, assess and publicise high quality studies, with a focus on those occurring in resource-limited settings. 

A total of 25 articles were identified for summary and critique. AKU's study which applied Clinical Respiratory Score as a measure to assess which children, who came to an ER with respiratory distress, had the greatest need for specialist treatment, was among the year's top studies.

The study looks into respiratory distress among children in a paediatric emergency department. The research focused on Clinical Respiratory Score (CRS) of 112 children aged between one-month to 16 years. The respiratory distress was assessed based on a combination of six parameters such as respiratory rate, presence of wheeze, complexion, oxygen saturation, use of accessory muscle, and mental status. 

The CRS was checked for consistency and based on the score, patients were divided into three categories: mild, moderate and severe which helped indicate if a child needed to be shifted to paediatric critical care (either intensive care or special care unit). 

The research concluded that a CRS of 3 and greater was able to distinguish between severe and non-severe illness. The CRS was originally known for ascertaining respiratory distress in paediatric patients with asthma and sickle cell anaemia in high-resource countries, but the study demonstrated its applicability in a low-resource country like Pakistan for paediatric respiratory distress for a number of causes.

The study was conducted at the Aga Khan University Hospital in Karachi without grant support.

"Our study making the cut for the top 5 per cent of global emergency medicine studies in 2018, per GEMLR, establishes that if your research team has the drive, passion, pertinent research question and a solid hypothesis, then you should go for it," said Asad Mian, an associate professor and chair of the department of emergency medicine at AKU. "If one is getting valuable preliminary data then the chances of getting a grant for a follow-up study go up." 

Members of the research team from AKU include Kanwal Nayani of the department of paediatrics and child health; Rubaba Naeem, Owais Munir, Naureen Naseer and Asher Feroze from the department of emergency medicine. Nick Brown from Uppsala University, Sweden, was also part of the study.
